nameStory: Greater celandine gets its name from the Greek word 'chelidon,' meaning swallow, because it was believed to bloom when swallows arrived in spring and fade when they departed in fall. The 'greater' part distinguishes it from lesser celandine, which is actually in a completely different plant family despite sharing the name.
description: Greater celandine is a knee-high herbaceous plant that's part of the poppy family, originally from Europe and Asia but now common throughout New England. It has deeply lobed, blue-green leaves and produces clusters of bright yellow, four-petaled flowers from late spring through summer. The plant typically grows 1-3 feet tall and has a somewhat weedy appearance, often found in disturbed or semi-shaded areas.

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Break a stem and bright orange-yellow sap immediately oozes out - this distinctive colored latex is the plant's signature feature and stains fingers easily

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly four rounded petals arranged in a cross pattern, about the size of a nickel, appearing in loose clusters

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Blue-green leaves that are deeply lobed with rounded segments, arranged alternately on the stem, feeling somewhat soft and having a slightly waxy texture

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright plant reaching 1-3 feet tall with branching stems that feel brittle and break easily when bent

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, narrow seed pods that split open along two seams to release small black seeds with white attachments

habitat: Greater celandine thrives in partially shaded, disturbed areas with moist, rich soil throughout New England. Look for it along woodland edges, near old foundations, in overgrown gardens, and along fence rows where soil has been enriched by human activity. It's particularly common around old homesteads and in areas where the forest floor has been disturbed.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges in April with the characteristic blue-green lobed leaves, followed by the first yellow flowers in late May.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with abundant four-petaled yellow flowers and the most obvious orange sap production when stems are broken.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to yellow and die back, with seed pods splitting open to release seeds before the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to the ground, leaving no visible trace above soil level.

funFact: Greater celandine's bright orange sap was historically used as a natural wart remover and was called 'wart wort' - the caustic latex actually can dissolve warts, though it's not recommended due to potential skin irritation and the plant's mildly toxic properties.
confusionNotes: Despite the name, greater celandine is completely unrelated to lesser celandine (a buttercup family plant with glossy heart-shaped leaves). The orange sap when stems are broken is the instant giveaway - no other common New England plant has this bright orange latex.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'celandine' causes significant confusion because lesser celandine and greater celandine are in completely different plant families and look quite different. Greater celandine is in the poppy family, while lesser celandine belongs to the buttercup family - they share only the common name due to both having yellow flowers.
compareHints: Greater celandine is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England. Within the poppy family, it's easily distinguished from other relatives like bloodroot by its orange sap (bloodroot has red sap), four-petaled yellow flowers (bloodroot has white flowers with 8+ petals), and its deeply lobed leaves versus bloodroot's rounded, palm-shaped leaves.
